children: OTTAWA--Canada's population grew only marginally in the latest quarter, with numbers swelling at the lowest pace since World War II and by less than when border restrictions were in place to combat the spread of Covid-19.

The country's population hit an estimated just under 41.8 million on July 1, a rise of 189,425 people, or 0.5%, on a year earlier, Statistics Canada said Wednesday. The population grew by 0.2% from the prior quarter.

After years of growth, Canada's population growth has cooled sharply in recent quarters after the federal government tightened immigration policy and cut numbers of temporary residents. Still, upward revisions to earlier estimates thanks in part to improved counting of temporary residents wiped out what had previously been calculated for 2025 as the first annual decline in the population for the country on record.

The annual July-to-July rise in the population is the lowest since 1944 to 1945, when the number of people in Canada climbed by about 126,000, and is the smallest in percentage terms since growth of 0.3% between the 1915 and 1916, the data agency said. The pace undershot the 0.6% growth in the population for the time of year during the height of the pandemic, between July 1, 2020, and the same date a year later.
On a quarterly basis, the population of the country increased by an estimated 80,343, which marked the lowest growth for the second quarter since 2020 just as the Covid-19 pandemic began.

Ottawa in late 2024 unveiled revised immigration targets. In an effort to further bring down immigration, Prime Minister Mark Carney's government stepped up the plans with a target of a more than 40% cut to the entry of temporary immigrants in 2026 and 2027 from current levels. That has been projected to lower the share of temporary immigrants to 5% of the population in 2027.

"We remain in an era of normalization, with population growth of just above zero expected through 2027, before settling back to a baseline of just under 1%," said Bank of Montreal senior economist Robert Kavcic.
Rapid shifts in Canada's population growth since 2020 have been almost entirely due to changes in international migration.
Immigrants welcomed into Canada dropped to 368,224, a fourth consecutive yearly decline for July and the first time since 2022 the annual number of immigrants has fallen below 400,000.

The number of non-permanent residents in Canada dropped by 154,614 people on an annual basis to reach 2.78 million on July 1, or 6.7% of the total population. This is down from a high of 2.98 million temporary residents on Oct. 1, 2024, or 7.2% of the total population. The largest decreases were among study-permit holders and work-and-study permit holders.
